content_html:
Buying a PDF pattern does not mean buying copyright in its content. In the EU, an original work receives copyright protection automatically when created, and the right holder controls uses such as reproduction and distribution subject to licenses and applicable exceptions.

This guide resolves the situation with practical criteria and avoids automatic fixes that can make the project worse or add unnecessary work.

What you buy with a pattern

Idea, method and original expression

It is important to separate an idea or method from its particular expression. Cross stitch methods, a blank grid or familiar symbols are not owned by one person; an original chart, illustrations, text and sufficiently creative layout may be protected.

Sharing or redistributing the PDF

Sharing, reselling or uploading the pattern file generally involves reproducing or distributing the work and should not be done without permission or a license that allows it. Paying for a copy does not make the digital file freely distributable.

Selling finished stitched items

Selling the physical stitched item is a different question and can depend on applicable law, the protected elements involved and the designer's license terms. Check the actual license rather than assuming one universal rule.

Designs based on third-party works

If a pattern depicts third-party characters, logos, artworks or photographs, additional rights can apply even when you created the grid yourself. Designing from your own, licensed or public-domain source material reduces risk.

Writing a clear license

This article can explain general principles but is not legal advice for a specific case. For our PDFs, we should use a clear license explaining file use, personal copies and any permissions relating to finished stitched items.

Overall, the best solution preserves stability, readability and a reasonable stitching experience. Our editorial content should explain why, and our patterns should apply the same judgment to materials, layout and working notes.

Copyright rules vary by jurisdiction, but one principle is broadly important: purchasing a pattern file normally gives you a copy under specific terms; it does not transfer ownership of the underlying copyright. The designer or other rights holder may still control reproduction, distribution and derivative uses. Always read the license supplied with the pattern and do not assume that payment makes the PDF freely shareable.

Sharing the digital chart is different from showing your finished stitching. Uploading the PDF, emailing copies to friends, posting readable chart pages or redistributing a scan can reproduce the protected work. A social photograph of the completed embroidery may be entirely different in legal and licensing terms from posting a high-resolution image that lets others reconstruct the pattern.

Selling a physical stitched item is more nuanced. Laws, licenses and the protected elements involved can differ, so there is no reliable one-sentence rule for every country and every design. Some designers explicitly permit small-scale sales of finished pieces, others set conditions, and third-party characters or artwork can introduce additional rights beyond the chart itself.

Public-domain source material also needs care. An old painting may no longer be protected by copyright, yet a modern photograph, edited scan, font or adaptation can have separate rights or contractual usage terms. Creating a cross-stitch conversion from a found image is therefore not automatically safe simply because the original artwork is old.

For MAKE, each PDF should include a plain-language license explaining personal copies, file sharing and any permission we choose to grant for finished stitched items. Clear terms reduce customer uncertainty and make enforcement fairer because buyers know the rules before they use the design commercially.

This article can provide general educational information, not legal advice for a specific dispute. When a project involves substantial commercial use, licensed characters, commissioned artwork or conflicting terms, the safest route is to check the applicable law and obtain appropriate professional advice rather than relying on a generic craft rule.

Licenses should be saved with the file when they contain important permissions. Product pages can change over time, and a buyer who later wants to sell a finished piece needs to know which terms accompanied the purchase. Keeping a dated copy or note avoids relying on memory.

Commissioned work needs its own agreement. Paying someone to draw a custom chart does not automatically answer who can reproduce, resell or adapt that design. If MAKE offers bespoke patterns, our terms should state what the customer may do with the finished PDF and whether we retain the design for portfolio or resale.

Copyright and trademark are different issues. A self-drawn chart of a protected brand logo may avoid copying another chart while still raising trademark or other rights questions. Original drawing alone does not automatically make every subject commercially unrestricted.
